topic: The page completes a criterion for continuity via fundamental sequences, then notes research problems on algebraic numbers satisfying linear differential equations, on proving the rationality of Bernoulli numbers from Riemann's zeta integral, and on proving Wiener's assertion about the special Pascal theorem.

triage.modern_statement: The sentence breaks off on this page, so the exact wording of Wiener's assertion is not visible. The reference is to Hermann Wiener's talk at the 1891 Halle meeting, 'Über Grundlagen und Aufbau der Geometrie', printed in the Jahresbericht der DMV, vol. 1. In that report Wiener says the incidence axioms of the projective plane alone cannot prove the theorems of Desargues and Pascal. Here 'special Pascal theorem' means the case of two lines, which is the Pappus theorem. In modern terms the problem is to prove that the Pappus (special Pascal) theorem is independent of the plane incidence and order axioms. Hilbert later sharpened this: Pappus does not follow even when Desargues and the other plane axioms are added, unless the Archimedean (continuity) axiom is also assumed. Equivalently, it asks for a projective plane, or an ordered non-Archimedean plane, coordinatized by a skew field that is not commutative, so that Desargues holds but Pappus fails.
triage.answered_by: David Hilbert himself, in Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899), the chapters on Desargues' and Pascal's theorems. He built a non-Archimedean geometry over a non-commutative ordered skew field in which Pappus/Pascal fails. He also showed that Pascal's theorem follows once the Archimedean axiom is assumed. Hilbert's Theorem 35 is a related result: a plane is Desarguesian exactly when it can be embedded in space. Moulton (Trans. AMS, 1902) notes that Wiener had already stated that result. Moulton also gave a simpler non-Desarguesian plane in which Pascal's theorem fails. F. Schur had derived Pascal's theorem from the spatial and congruence axioms without the Archimedean axiom.

evidence.claim: A historical survey says Wiener's brief report (1892) states that the projective-plane axioms do not allow a proof of Desargues' or Pascal's theorem ('Der Beweis dieser Sätze kann nicht ...').

Hilbert attended the DMV meeting in Halle in September 1891, where Hermann Wiener lectured on the foundations of geometry. Hilbert's own work closely examined the role of each axiom group in proving the theorems of Desargues and Pappus.

Moulton (1902) says that Hilbert's Grundlagen Theorem 35 (the condition for a plane geometry to be Desarguesian) 'was stated by H. Wiener: Jahresbericht DMV vol. 1, p. 47'. He shows that Pascal's theorem is not a consequence of Hilbert's plane axioms, and notes that Hilbert proved it follows from certain axioms.
Schur proved Pascal's theorem from the spatial and congruence axioms without the Archimedean axiom, and this inspired Hilbert's return to the foundations of geometry.
Hilbert's Grundlagen der Geometrie (English translation) builds non-Archimedean geometries to prove independence results.

triage.why: The Halle reference clearly points to Wiener's 1891 talk, and the topic (whether the Pascal/Pappus theorem can be proved from the plane axioms) is a classic question in the foundations of geometry. Hilbert settled it in Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899), and it is now standard: Pappus is equivalent to commutative coordinates, while Desargues gives only a skew field. It is not one of the 23 problems. Confidence is medium for three reasons. The note ends before Wiener's claim is complete, so whether he meant 'without continuity' or 'without space/congruence' cannot be fixed from this page. Wiener's original text is known to me only through a secondary source. Searches ran out before I could get a direct quote of Hilbert's Pascal-independence theorem.
